chunks: GPIO pin circuit and operation. The question: Draw a GPIO circuit. How does it work?
Inside a GPIO pin, two switches connect to its metal contact, the pad. One switch joins it to the supply voltage. The other joins it to ground.
Close the top switch and the pin is high. Close the bottom one and the pin is low. Open both and the pin is an input, because it is no longer driven.
A small sensing circuit, the input buffer, reads the pad's voltage. Protective diodes complete the circuit.
Picture a pipe junction with two taps. The top tap connects to a tank of water at supply level. The bottom tap connects to a drain.
Open the top tap and the pipe fills, which is high. Open the bottom tap and it drains, which is low. Close both and the pipe is free, so you can read its water level from outside.
Relief valves on the pipe vent any dangerous overpressure.
The gating that creates three output states from two bits. When OE is 0, NAND gives 1 (PMOS off) and NOR gives 0 (NMOS off): high impedance.
When OE is 1, both gates see the inverse of D.
PMOS and NMOS: two kinds of transistor, used as electrically controlled switches. The PMOS joins the pad to the supply. The NMOS joins it to ground.
High impedance (high-Z): both switches off. The pin neither drives nor loads the wire. This is input mode. Clamp diode: a diode that conducts when the pad goes about 0.
7 volts beyond the supply or ground, steering the extra current away.
Say each switch has about 25 ohms of resistance when on. With data 1, the top switch conducts and the pad sits near 3. 3 volts.
With data 0, the bottom one conducts and the pad sits near 0 volts. Now suppose two such pins on one wire disagree. Current flows through both switches: 3.
3 over (25 plus 25) equals 66 milliamps, far too much. Likewise, 5 volts on a 3. 3 volts pin not rated for it turns on the upper diode and pushes current into the supply.
That is the whole idea.
"The pad connects to a CMOS pair: a PMOS to VDD and an NMOS to ground, driven by the output data and an enable.
Data 1 turns on the PMOS and pulls high, data 0 turns on the NMOS and pulls low, and with the enable off both are off, so the pin is high impedance, which is input mode.
The input goes through a Schmitt-trigger buffer into the input register.
There are optional pull-up and pull-down resistors with switches, and two ESD diodes, one to VDD and one to ground, to clamp overvoltage. Configuration registers choose the mode."
